name: Son Clave 3-2
story: The spine of every Cuban son, salsa, and half of Latin music since 1800.

name: Bembé
story: The 12/8 bell that underlies bembé, abakuá, and half the West African diaspora.

name: Rumba Clave 3-2
story: Rumba's clave — the three-side's last stroke comes one 16th later than son. That delay is everything.

name: Bolero Cubano
story: The Cuban ballad — slow, tender, and built around the trova tradition of moonlit guitar serenades.

name: Cha-Cha-Chá
story: Violinist Enrique Jorrín slowed the mambo down so everybody could dance. The name comes from dancers' shuffling feet.

name: Mambo
story: The climax section of any salsa arrangement — when the band opens up and the mambo bell takes over.

name: Guaguancó
story: The most popular form of rumba — a secular ritual born in Havana courtyards, where a male dancer pursues a female dancer in stylized courtship.

name: Rumba Columbia
story: The fastest, most virtuosic rumba — a solo male dance of acrobatic and sometimes dangerous moves, rooted in Abakuá sacred rhythms from Calabar.

name: Comparsa
story: The costumed carnival processions of Santiago — frying pans mounted on blocks, cowbells, and a river of drums rolling through the streets.

name: Cáscara
story: Played on the side of a timbal — slinky, sideways, reserved for mambo verses before the montuno opens up.

name: Son Clave 2-3
story: Son clave flipped — two side first, then three. Most Cuban charts start here because the melodic phrasing anticipates the "3" resolution.

name: Danzón
story: Cuba's national dance in 1879 — a ballroom form built on the cinquillo (3+3+2 sub-divisional cell). The timbale's baqueteo pattern is the rhythmic spine.

name: Songo
story: Changuito invented songo with Los Van Van in the 1970s — the first Cuban rhythm conceived for the drum set, fusing rumba, son, funk and jazz drumming.

name: Timba
story: NG La Banda, Los Van Van, Paulito FG — aggressive, funk-influenced, gear-shifting evolution of salsa. The kick drum arrives and the music gets denser.

name: Yambú
story: The oldest and slowest rumba — originally played on wooden shipping-crate cajones, imitating the movements of elderly people. No vacunao, no hurry.

name: Pilón
story: Enrique Bonne and Pacho Alonso built a dance craze around the pilón — the mortar used to grind sugar cane. The choreography imitates the pounding motion.

name: Changüí
story: The father of son. In the eastern sugar plantations of Guantánamo the bongó was the timeline — wilder, more improvisatory, more West African than the son that would follow.

name: Mozambique
story: Pedro "Pello el Afrokán" Izquierdo invented the mozambique for Havana's 1960s carnival. It crossed the straits to Eddie Palmieri and lit up New York salsa.

name: Bomba Sicá
story: The most widespread bomba style, built on the 3-3-2 tresillo. In bomba the dancer leads and the subidor drummer must follow — the conversation is the music.

name: Bomba Holandé
story: The 6/8 bomba that links Puerto Rican tradition back to West Africa. "Holandé" may nod to Dutch colonial traders — the rhythm sways like ocean swells.

name: Plena
story: "El periódico cantado" — the sung newspaper. Three hand-held panderos trade rhythms over Ponce's working-class streets, narrating whatever happened this week.

name: Merengue
story: The national rhythm of the Dominican Republic — tambora and güira against an accordion. Trujillo promoted it as a tool of the state; the country made it a birthright.

name: Charanga
story: The charanga francesa — wooden flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales and güiro — was the elegant Cuban orchestra that birthed danzón, cha-cha and pachanga. Enrique Jorrín's Orquesta América shaped mid-century Havana dancing.

name: Danzón-Chá
story: The slower third section that opens out of a classic danzón — the baqueteo softens and the dancers step wider. The bridge between Cuba's Belle Époque ballroom and Jorrín's cha-cha-chá.

name: Mambo-Rumba
story: When the Palladium-era big bands brought guaguancó into the mambo arrangement — rumba clave sharpening the mambo's attack while the bell section churns on underneath.

name: Son Montuno
story: Arsenio Rodríguez electrified son in the 1940s — added conga, piano, a trumpet section. Montuno is the open call-and-response section where the band gears up. Everything that became salsa passes through here.

name: Afro 6/8
story: The modern ensemble's take on the Yoruba bell — bembé translated to drum kit and bass for Afro-Cuban jazz and timba's 6/8 passages. Chucho Valdés, Irakere, Gonzalo Rubalcaba live in this meter.

name: Iyesá
story: The Iyesá are Yoruba descendants in Matanzas whose ritual drums preserve Ijesha regional rhythms from Nigeria. Four single-headed drums tuned by cords, an iron bell on top — a tradition older than recorded Cuba.

name: Abakuá
story: The only African secret society re-established in the Americas — founded Havana 1836 from the Efik/Ejagham Ekpe. The bonkó enchemiyá lead drum speaks over obi-apá shoulder drums; the sacred ekue friction drum stays hidden.

name: Palo / Yuka
story: The Kongo-descended yuka drums of western Cuba — "yuka" means "to beat" in Bantu. Paired with the makuta, they underpin Las Reglas de Congo. Trance-inducing, driving, repetitive — the aesthetic of Central African ritual.

name: Guaguancó Habanero
story: The Havana style of guaguancó — faster and more volatile than Matanzas, born in the solares (tenement courtyards) of the capital. Los Papines and Yoruba Andabo define the lineage.

name: Guaguancó Matancero
story: The Matanzas style of guaguancó — slower, more ritualistic, drier timbre on cajones. Los Muñequitos de Matanzas carry this lineage where Havana players push tempo, Matanceros hold the space.

name: Cáscara (full timbale shell)
story: The real cáscara — the 11-stroke figure a timbalero plays on the shell of the timbales during son montuno sections. The simplified version (see cascara) reduces this to backbeat snare for drum-kit translation; this is the dense original that rides next to the clave and cowbell.
